newsitem.title: ITALY: Mobsters cash in on Albanian exodus, Italy frets.
newsitem.headline: Mobsters cash in on Albanian exodus, Italy frets.

text.p: The Italian government said on Tuesday mobsters had muscled in on the latest Albanian exodus as bedraggled refugees described how they paid racketeers hundreds of dollars to cross the Adriatic.
More than 8,000 Albanian refugees have made the short sea crossing in a ramshackle flotilla of rusty boats over the past five days and United Nations officials in Geneva said the pace was picking up.
"This is a business run by organised crime," said Giannicola Sinisi, undersecretary at the interior ministry, who was in the south eastern region of Puglia to monitor the situation.
The president of Puglia's regional council, Salvatore Distaso, called on the government to declare a state of emergency in the area, saying it could not cope with the influx.
Exhausted passengers reaching Italy said they paid the equivalent of $600 each in the port of Durres for places on jam-packed vessels and voyages to a new life abroad.

"I paid and I would pay again if I had to," said Aljosha Sulaj, a 28-year-old businessman who said he had handed over the equivalent of around $3,000 for himself, his wife, his mother-in-law and their young son and baby daughter.
The average monthly wage in Albania is around $65.
"To get to the port was not easy. At every checkpoint there were people with guns who asked for money and I gave it to them. Then there was no problem getting near the boat," he said.
Reporters in Durres said more vessels, one without engines, set off in the morning with hundreds of emigrants aboard.
The U.S. navy said on Tuesday it had saved 20 Albanian men who had been drifting in a boat in the Adriatic Sea for five days, three of them without food and water.

A statement from a U.S. Marine task force in the Adriatic said the 20 men abandoned their powerless 25-foot vessel, which was taking on water, when a rescue boat from the cruiser Leyte Gulf pulled alongside late on Monday afternoon.
It added that the group would be sent to Brindisi.

Chief anti-Mafia prosecutor Pier Luigi Vigna said he was worried that the influx of Albanians would lift the crime rate, as many of Albania's jails were empty after rioters stormed prisons and opened the gates.

"The Albanian mafia is running the boats in Durres...Our worry is that, apart from the Albanian mafia, Albanian arms will come in too -- arms that will then become available to the (Italian) mafia," Vigna told Corriere della Sera newspaper.
Italy faced a crisis in 1991 when some 40,000 Albanians commandeered rusting freighters and poured across the Adriatic after the collapse of 45 years of Stalinist rule.
It has since grappled with continuing problems of illegal Albanian immigration and drugs and arms-smuggling.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government says it will grant temporary sanctuary to genuine refugees from the armed chaos that has swept the country in an eruption of anger over the failure of shady saving schemes.
Prodi called a cabinet meeting for Wednesday to discuss how to cope with the latest wave of Albanians to wash ashore.
Makeshift reception centres in the southeast are full to capacity, Albanians are being moved to other regions, and the mood of Italians in the past two days has turned from sympathy to suspicion.
"This is not a flight of the desperate," La Repubblica newspaper wrote. "This is the emigration of people who hope that they can seize the opportunity to get here and stay."
